claim: Jellyfish nerve nets provide insight into the origins of nervous systems due to their taxonomic position and evolutionary age.
source: Jellyfish nerve nets provide insight into the origins of nervous systems, as both their taxonomic position and their evolutionary age imply that jellyfish resemble some of the earliest neuron-bearing, actively-swimming animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to established scientific knowledge about jellyfish phylogeny and evolution.

claim: Cnidarians and ctenophores are the only non-bilaterian animal phyla with neurons.
source: Cnidarians (in particular jellyfish) and ctenophores (comb jellies) are the only non-bilaterian animal phyla with neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific consensus about animal phylogeny and neuron distribution.

claim: Evidence suggests that cnidarians are our most distant relatives with homologous neurons and muscles.
source: While their phylogenetic position is still not entirely resolved, evidence suggests that cnidarians are our most distant relatives with homologous neurons and muscles (Steinmetz et al., 2012; Marlow and Arendt, 2014; Moroz and Kohn, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Well-preserved fossils of medusozoa exist from the Cambrian.
source: Well-preserved fossils of medusozoa from the Cambrian (Cartwright et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Evidence for medusoid forms exists from the Ediacaran.
source: evidence for medusoid forms from the Ediacaran (Van Iten et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Jellyfish are evolutionary old.
source: Well-preserved fossils of medusozoa from the Cambrian (Cartwright et al., 2007) and evidence for medusoid forms from the Ediacaran (Van Iten et al., 2006) indicate that jellyfish are evolutionary old.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to fossil evidence.

claim: Jellyfish are similar to the earliest neuron-bearing, actively swimming animals.
source: These findings and their anatomical simplicity suggest that they are similar to the earliest neuron-bearing, actively swimming animals.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from fossil evidence and anatomical observations.

claim: The study of jellyfish should yield insight into the earliest nervous systems and behaviors.
source: Their study should therefore yield insight into the earliest nervous systems and behaviors.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the evolutionary position of jellyfish.

claim: The nervous system of scyphozoan jellyfish consists of several neuronal networks distributed over the entire jellyfish bell, tentacles, and endoderm.
source: The nervous system of scyphozoan jellyfish consists of several neuronal networks, which are distributed over the entire jellyfish bell, the tentacles and the endoderm (Schäfer, 1878; Passano and Passano, 1971).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Rhopalia are small sensory structures of which there are usually eight distributed around the margin of the bell.
source: The only obvious points of concentration of a larger number of neurons are the rhopalia (Figure 1), small sensory structures of which there are usually eight distributed around the margin of the bell (Nakanishi et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1.

claim: During the swimming motion almost all the subumbrellar muscles contract synchronously and push the jellyfish forward.
source: During the swimming motion almost all the subumbrellar muscles contract synchronously and push the jellyfish forward.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about jellyfish swimming.

claim: Romanes found that the contraction usually starts at one of the rhopalia and propagates around almost arbitrarily placed cuts in the subumbrella.
source: In a series of cutting experiments, Romanes destroyed and removed parts of the umbrella. He found that the contraction usually starts at one of the rhopalia and propagates around almost arbitrarily placed cuts in the subumbrella.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Romanes' experimental work.

claim: Romanes observed two different types of contraction waves: a fast, strong wave leading to the regular swimming motion and a slower wave at about half the speed.
source: Furthermore, Romanes observed two different types of contraction waves: a fast, strong wave leading to the regular swimming motion and a slower wave, at about half the speed, which was so weak that one could hardly see it activate the swim musculature.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Romanes' experimental observations.

claim: When a slow contraction wave reached a rhopalium, a fast excitation wave emerged from that rhopalium after a short delay.
source: When a slow contraction wave originating somewhere on the outer margin of the jellyfish umbrella reached a rhopalium, a fast excitation wave emerged from that rhopalium after a short delay.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Romanes' experimental observations.

claim: Two different nerve nets, the motor nerve net (MNN) and the diffuse nerve net (DNN), are responsible for the fast and slow contraction wave, respectively.
source: With advancing neurobiological methods, Romanes' observations were later verified and expanded (Passano, 1965; Satterlie, 2002). This led to the identification of two different nerve nets, the motor nerve net (MNN) and the diffuse nerve net (DNN), which are responsible for the fast and slow contraction wave, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The motor nerve net extends over the subumbrella.
source: The motor nerve net extends over the subumbrella (Figure 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1.

claim: The motor nerve net consists of large neurons with usually two neurites.
source: The motor nerve net extends over the subumbrella (Figure 1) and consists of large neurons with usually two neurites (Schäfer, 1878; Anderson and Schwab, 1981; Satterlie, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: MNN neurons function in basically the same manner as neurons with chemical synapses in higher animals.
source: The neurons function in basically the same manner as neurons with chemical synapses in higher animals (Anderson and Schwab, 1983; Anderson, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The MNN is through-conducting in the sense that if a small number of neurons is activated, a wave of activation spreads over the entire network.
source: The MNN is through-conducting in the sense that if a small number of neurons is activated, a wave of activation spreads over the entire network, leading to a series of neuronal discharges.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MNN properties.

claim: The conduction speed in the MNN is between 45 cm/s and 1 m/s.
source: The conduction speed is between 45 cm/s and 1 m/s (Horridge, 1956; Passano, 1965).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The activation in the MNN is preserved even if large parts of the network are destroyed.
source: The activation is preserved even if large parts of the network are destroyed.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MNN robustness.

claim: MNN activation generates Romanes' fast contracting wave in the swim musculature.
source: It generates Romanes' fast contracting wave in the swim musculature (Horridge, 1956).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Spontaneous waves in the MNN are initiated by pacemakers located in each of the rhopalia.
source: Spontaneous waves in the MNN are initiated by pacemakers located in each of the rhopalia (Passano, 1965).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: After firing, the wave-initiating pacemaker resets and the other ones reset due to the arriving MNN activity.
source: After firing, the wave-initiating pacemaker resets and the other ones reset due to the arriving MNN activity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about pacemaker dynamics.

claim: Sensory input modulates the pacemaker activity.
source: Horridge (1959) showed that sensory input modulates the pacemaker activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Sensory input modulation of pacemaker activity may be one of the main mechanisms of sensory integration and creation of controlled motor output in the jellyfish.
source: This may be one of the main mechanisms of sensory integration and creation of controlled motor output in the jellyfish.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the role of sensory modulation.

claim: MNN synapses are symmetrical, both morphologically and functionally.
source: First, even though the synapses seem to be exclusively chemical they are symmetrical, both morphologically and functionally.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MNN synapses.

claim: Both sides of the MNN synaptic cleft have a similar structure containing vesicles as well as receptors.
source: Both sides of the synaptic cleft have a similar structure containing vesicles as well as receptors (Horridge and Mackay, 1962).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: MNN neurites do not differentiate into axon and dendrite.
source: In particular, the neurites do not differentiate into axon and dendrite.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about MNN neurite structure.

claim: The conduction in the MNN is bidirectional.
source: Anderson (1985) directly showed that the conduction is bidirectional.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Electrical synapses have not been found in the MNN, neither through staining nor in electrophysiological experiments.
source: Electrical synapses have not been found, neither through staining nor in electrophysiological experiments (Anderson and Schwab, 1981; Anderson, 1985; Anderson and Spencer, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: MNN synapses are strong, usually creating an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) that induces an action potential (AP) in the receiving neuron.
source: Second, synapses are strong, usually creating an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) that induces an action potential (AP) in the receiving neuron (Anderson, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The MNN remains robustly through-conducting during cutting experiments.
source: This fits with the observation that the MNN remains robustly through-conducting during cutting experiments (Horridge, 1954b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The refractory period of scyphozoan neurons is initially absolute for about 30 ms and thereafter relative for about 70 ms.
source: This is likely due to the long refractory period of scyphozoan neurons, which is initially absolute for about 30 ms and thereafter relative for about 70 ms (Anderson and Schwab, 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The conduction speed of DNN activity waves along the subumbrella is 15 cm/s.
source: The conduction speed of activity waves (15 cm/s) along the subumbrella is less than in the MNN (Passano, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Horridge was the first to suggest that innervation of the swim musculature via the DNN with its slower time scale may allow for a different activation pattern and thereby induce a turning motion.
source: Horridge (1956) was the first to suggest that innervation of the swim musculature via the DNN with its slower time scale may allow for a different activation pattern and thereby induce a turning motion.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: No visible contraction of the regular swim musculature after DNN excitation was observed in Aurelia.
source: In Aurelia, however, no visible contraction of the regular swim musculature after DNN excitation was observed (Horridge, 1956).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The DNN might influence the circular muscles by amplifying the impact of the MNN activity as measured in other jellyfish.
source: Still, the DNN might influence the circular muscles by amplifying the impact of the MNN activity as it was measured in other jellyfish (Passano, 1965; Passano, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature and involves speculation.

claim: There is a small band of radial muscles on the marginal angles of Aurelia, which contract during a turning motion.
source: In addition, there is a small band of radial muscles on the marginal angles of Aurelia, which contract during a turning motion (Gemmell et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The speed of the muscle activation and the position of the muscles indicate that they are innervated by the DNN.
source: The speed of the muscle activation and the position of the muscles indicate that they are innervated by the DNN.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: DNN activity can activate the MNN indirectly via a rhopalium.
source: In accordance with the idea of a coupled activation of DNN and MNN, DNN activity can activate the MNN indirectly via a rhopalium.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about nerve net interactions.

claim: The delay observed between DNN activity arrival and the initiation of the MNN activation is highly variable.
source: The delay observed between DNN activity arrival and the initiation of the MNN activation is highly variable (Passano, 1965; Passano, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The DNN does not directly interact with the MNN.
source: Apart from this, the DNN does not directly interact with the MNN (Horridge, 1956).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Some behavioral and anatomical evidence suggests that a rhopalium might activate the DNN together with the MNN in response to a strong sensory stimulus.
source: Some behavioral (Horridge, 1956; Gemmell et al., 2015) and anatomical (Nakanishi et al., 2009) evidence suggests that a rhopalium might activate the DNN together with the MNN in response to a strong sensory stimulus.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature and involves speculation.

claim: Oblate-shaped jellyfish like Aurelia are among the most efficient swimmers in the world.
source: Oblate-shaped jellyfish like Aurelia are among the most efficient swimmers in the world.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about jellyfish swimming efficiency.

claim: The cost of transport of oblate-shaped jellyfish is very low.
source: Their cost of transport (energy consumption during movement per mass and movement distance) is very low (Gemmell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Jellyfish do not have muscles that actively open the bell after a contraction.
source: Jellyfish do not have muscles that actively open the bell after a contraction.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about jellyfish anatomy.

claim: The jellyfish body is filled with mesoglea, a mixture of fluid and elastic fibers that create a hydrostatic skeleton.
source: Instead their body is filled with mesoglea, a mixture of fluid and elastic fibers that create a hydrostatic skeleton.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about jellyfish anatomy.

claim: During a contraction the mesoglea stores elastic energy created by pushing the fluid to the center and stretching the fibers, which leads to relaxation of the bell when the muscle tension drops.
source: During a contraction the mesoglea stores elastic energy created by pushing the fluid to the center and stretching the fibers, which leads to relaxation of the bell when the muscle tension drops (Alexander, 1964; Gladfelter, 1972; Gladfelter, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The specific swimming mechanism of oblate jellyfish has been described as 'rowing' or 'paddling', as opposed to 'jetting', which is found in prolate jellyfish.
source: The specific swimming mechanism of oblate jellyfish has been described as 'rowing' or 'paddling', as opposed to 'jetting', which is found in prolate jellyfish (Colin and Costello, 2002; Sahin et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Jellyfish that use the jetting swimming mechanism produce most of their forward momentum during their contraction phase.
source: Jellyfish that use the latter swimming mechanism produce most of their forward momentum during their contraction phase, and get pushed forward by propelling fluid out of their bell (Villanueva et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Rowers produce their forward momentum through a series of vortex rings at the bell margin.
source: In contrast rowers produce their forward momentum through a series of vortex rings at the bell margin.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about rowing jellyfish swimming.

claim: Vortices form both during the contraction and the relaxation of the bell in rowing jellyfish.
source: Since these vortices form both during the contraction and the relaxation of the bell, rowers are highly cost efficient swimmers (Colin and Costello, 2002; Dabiri et al., 2005; Dabiri et al., 2007; Gemmell et al., 2013; Gemmell et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Rowers are highly cost efficient swimmers.
source: Since these vortices form both during the contraction and the relaxation of the bell, rowers are highly cost efficient swimmers (Colin and Costello, 2002; Dabiri et al., 2005; Dabiri et al., 2007; Gemmell et al., 2013; Gemmell et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The Immersed Boundary (IB) method has been applied to study the interactions of aquatic animals with the surrounding fluid.
source: Methods like the Immersed Boundary (IB) method have been applied to study the interactions of aquatic animals with the surrounding fluid (Fauci and Peskin, 1988; Peskin, 2002; Cortez et al., 2004; Bhalla et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: In anguilliform swimmers, the same muscle activation patterns can produce different swimming motions depending on body stiffness.
source: This revealed for example that in anguilliform swimmers, the same muscle activation patterns can produce different swimming motions depending on body stiffness (Tytell and Lauder, 2004; Tytell et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Jellyfish turn by creating an asymmetric bell contraction.
source: Jellyfish turn by creating an asymmetric bell contraction (Gladfelter, 1973).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: In most scyphozoan jellyfish, the part of the bell on the inner side of the turn contracts stronger and earlier.
source: In most scyphozoan jellyfish, the part of the bell on the inner side of the turn contracts stronger and earlier (Gladfelter, 1973; Horridge, 1956).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Horridge suggested that asymmetric contraction is because the activities of DNN and MNN coincide on the inner side of the turn.
source: Horridge suggested that this is because the activities of DNN and MNN coincide there.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Horridge's work and involves speculation.

claim: The contraction wave during turning usually starts at the rhopalium on the inside of the turn.
source: The contraction wave then usually starts at the rhopalium on the inside of the turn (Shanks and Graham, 1987; Horridge, 1956).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Hoover created a 3D model of a jellyfish and tested the effect of a rectangular region of increased tension traveling in both directions around the bell.
source: Hoover created a 3D model of a jellyfish and tested the effect of a rectangular region of increased tension traveling in both directions around the bell.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoover's work.

claim: Hoover found that the bell turns toward the direction of the origin of the traveling wave.
source: He found that the bell turns toward the direction of the origin of this traveling wave, as observed in real jellyfish.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoover's work.

claim: The amount of angular displacement in Hoover's model depends strongly on the speed at which the activity travels around the bell.
source: The amount of angular displacement depends strongly on the speed at which the activity travels around the bell.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hoover's work.

claim: During regular swimming, the margins of Aurelia are very flexible and follow the rest of the bell as it contracts and expands.
source: During regular swimming, the margins of Aurelia are very flexible and follow the rest of the bell as it contracts and expands (McHenry and Jed, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Robot and 3D models show that flexible bell margins enhance the performance of swimming by increasing the vorticity of the vortex rings that are shed off.
source: Robot and 3D models show that such 'flaps' enhance the performance of swimming by increasing the vorticity of the vortex rings that are shed off (Colin et al., 2012; Villanueva et al., 2014; Hoover et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: During turning maneuvers the bell margins in Aurelia stiffen, starting at the origin of the activation wave.
source: During turning maneuvers they stiffen the margins, starting at the origin of the activation wave (Gemmell et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The model current traces agree well with the measured ones, both qualitatively and quantitatively, for the broad experimentally explored range of clamping from −20 mV to +90 mV.
source: The current traces of the biophysical model agree well with the measured ones, both qualitatively and quantitatively, for the broad experimentally explored range of clamping from −20 mV to +90 mV (step-size: 7.5 mV, resting potential: −70 mV).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: The model generates APs similar to the ones observed experimentally by Anderson and Schwab (1983).
source: Our model generates APs similar to the ones observed experimentally by Anderson and Schwab (1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model output to experimental data.

claim: Before an AP, the leak current dominates.
source: Before an AP, the leak current dominates.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: After the voltage surpasses the inflection point, the fast transient in- and outward currents generate the voltage spike.
source: After the voltage surpasses the inflection point, the fast transient in- and outward currents generate the voltage spike.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: During the spike, the steady-state outward current activates and stays active during repolarization.
source: During the spike, the steady-state outward current activates and stays active during repolarization.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The slow outward current does not activate during the spike, since it requires depolarizations beyond +55 mV.
source: The slow outward current does not activate, since it requires depolarizations beyond +55 mV (Anderson, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data and citation to experimental observations.

claim: Model EPSCs have fast initial rise, initially fast and subsequently slow decay.
source: As experimentally observed in scyphozoan MNN neurons (Anderson, 1985), our model EPSCs have fast initial rise, initially fast and subsequently slow decay
evidence: The claim is supported by model design and comparison to experimental observations.

claim: A single EPSC suffices to evoke an AP in a resting neuron in the model.
source: and a single EPSC suffices to evoke an AP in a resting neuron (Anderson, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by model design and comparison to experimental observations.

claim: The model incorporates the experimentally observed synaptic rectification.
source: Furthermore, we incorporate the experimentally observed synaptic rectification: the synaptic current influx decays to zero when the voltage approaches the reversal potential (+4 mV) but does not reverse beyond (cf. brown trace in Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by model design and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: Synaptic transmission is activated when a neuron reaches +20 mV from below, which happens during spikes only.
source: Synaptic transmission is activated when a neuron reaches +20 mV from below, which happens during spikes only.
evidence: The claim is supported by model design.

claim: After transmitter release into the synaptic cleft, both pre- and postsynaptic neurons receive an EPSC in the model.
source: Since synapses in MNN neurons are symmetrical (Anderson, 1985; Anderson and Grünert, 1988), we hypothesize that after transmitter release into the synaptic cleft, both pre- and postsynaptic neurons receive an EPSC.
evidence: The claim is based on a hypothesis derived from experimental observations about synaptic symmetry.

claim: In the model, the 'synaptic reflux' is responsible for a delayed repolarisation.
source: In our model, this 'synaptic reflux' is responsible for a delayed repolarisation: the voltage stays near zero for several milliseconds after the fast return from the spike peak, see Figure 2B.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Delayed repolarization is also visible in electrophysiological recordings.
source: This is also visible in electrophysiological recordings (Anderson and Schwab, 1983; Anderson, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Experiments in two-neuron systems do not observe repetitive firing but only bumps of depolarization after a spike.
source: However, experiments in two-neuron systems do not observe such repetitive firing but only bumps of depolarization after a spike (Anderson, 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: The model does not observe repetitive firing in systems of two synaptically connected model neurons, but only bumps of depolarization after a spike.
source: In agreement with experimental findings, we do not observe repetitive firing in systems of two synaptically connected model neurons, but only bumps of depolarization after a spike.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data.

claim: The model neurons have a sufficiently long refractory period.
source: This indicates that our model neurons have a sufficiently long refractory period, although it has not been explicitly inserted.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model behavior.

claim: The model finds a refractory period of about 20 ms effective under arrival of synaptic inputs.
source: We find a refractory period of about 20 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The synaptic reflux and the steady-state current are crucial for the long duration of the effective refractory period.
source: We find that the synaptic reflux and the steady-state current are crucial for the long duration: without them the refractory period is reduced to about 5 ms (purple trace in Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Deactivation of the synaptic rectifier does not shorten the refractory period, but reduces the amplitude of the action potential.
source: In contrast, deactivation of the synaptic rectifier does not shorten the refractory period, but reduces the amplitude of the action potential, since the reversal potential of the channels is +4 mV.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The synaptic rectifier allows spike peaks to more clearly exceed the +20 mV threshold for synaptic transmission activation.
source: The synaptic rectifier thus allows spike peaks to more clearly exceed the +20 mV threshold for synaptic transmission activation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: The synaptic rectifier may increase the reliability of signal conduction in the MNN.
source: It may therefore increase the reliability of signal conduction in the MNN.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation derived from model results.

claim: During the activation wave following an arbitrary initial stimulation of the network, every neuron spikes exactly once.
source: In fact, the properties of the MNN indicate that during the activation wave following an arbitrary initial stimulation of the network, every neuron spikes exactly once.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the qualitative properties of the MNN.

claim: In a network where (i) the synapses are bidirectional, (ii) a presynaptic action potential evokes action potentials in all non-refractory postsynaptic neurons and (iii) the refractory period is so long that there is no repetitive firing in two neuron systems, every neuron will fire exactly once after initial stimulation.
source: Generally, this is the case in a network where (i) the synapses are bidirectional, (ii) a presynaptic action potential evokes action potentials in all non-refractory postsynaptic neurons and (iii) the refractory period is so long that there is no repetitive firing in two neuron systems.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from network properties.

claim: Numerical simulations confirm that firing of a pacemaker initiates a wave of activation where every MNN neuron generates exactly one AP.
source: Our numerical simulations confirm that firing of a pacemaker initiates a wave of activation where every MNN neuron generates exactly one AP (see Figures 5 and 6 for an illustration).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The activity propagates in two branches around the bell and these cancel each other on the opposite side.
source: The activity propagates in two branches around the bell. These cancel each other on the opposite side.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: During the wave, all other pacemakers fire as well, which presumably resets them in real jellyfish.
source: During the wave, all other pacemakers fire as well, which presumably resets them in real jellyfish.
evidence: The claim is based on model simulation data and speculation about real jellyfish.

claim: In a uniform MNN the wave spreads rather uniformly.
source: In a uniform MNN the wave spreads rather uniformly (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: In a von Mises MNN, the signal travels fastest around the center of the jellyfish and spreads from there, sometimes traveling a little backwards before extinguishing.
source: In a von Mises MNN, the signal travels fastest around the center of the jellyfish and spreads from there, sometimes traveling a little backwards before extinguishing (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Gemmell et al. (2015) observed a delay between the muscle contractions on the initiating and the opposite side of about 30 ms (std. dev. 14 ms), in Aurelia aurita of 3–4 cm diameter.
source: Gemmell et al. (2015) observed a delay between the muscle contractions on the initiating and the opposite side of about 30 ms (std. dev. 14 ms), in Aurelia aurita of 3–4 cm diameter.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: Both von Mises and uniform MNNs can generate delays within one standard deviation of the measurements by Gemmell et al. (2015).
source: We find that both our von Mises and uniform MNNs can generate delays within one standard deviation of the measurements, see Figure 4B.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Simulations indicate that MNN networks typically have 4000 neurons or more.
source: Our simulations indicate that MNN networks typically have 4000 neurons or more, as the propagation delays obtained for jellyfish with 3 and 4 cm diameter start to clearly bracket the experimentally found average at this size.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The delay between spiking of the initiating pacemaker and the opposing one decreases with neuron density.
source: Figure 4B shows that the delay decreases with neuron density.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In denser networks, the fastest path from the initiating pacemaker to the opposing one will be better approximated.
source: On the one hand, this is because in denser networks among the more synaptic partners of a neuron there will be some with better positions for fast wave propagation; in other words, the fastest path from the initiating pacemaker to the opposing one will be better approximated, if the neurons have more synaptic partners to which the activity propagates.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: There is a decrease of delay due to stronger stimulation of neurons in denser networks.
source: On the other hand, there is a decrease of delay due to stronger stimulation of neurons in denser networks: a postsynaptic neuron fires earlier if more presynaptic neurons have fired, since their EPSCs add up.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: Both von Mises and uniform MNNs reach similar propagation speeds with the same number of neurons.
source: Both von Mises and uniform MNNs reach similar propagation speeds with the same number of neurons (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Von Mises MNNs have fewer synapses than uniform MNNs with the same number of neurons.
source: but von Mises MNNs have fewer synapses (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Von Mises MNNs create more optimal paths of conduction than uniform MNNs.
source: This implies that von Mises MNNs create more optimal paths of conduction.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: Neurons near the pacemaker in von Mises MNNs preferably orient themselves radially towards the center of the subumbrella, and thus quickly direct the activity toward the opposite side.
source: Indeed, neurons near the pacemaker preferably orient themselves radially towards the center of the subumbrella, and thus quickly direct the activity toward the opposite side.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model structure and simulation data.

claim: Von Mises networks are more efficient for fast through-conduction than uniform ones.
source: Since transmitter release consumes a significant amount of energy (Niven, 2016), we conclude that von Mises networks are more efficient for fast through-conduction than uniform ones.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data and citation to literature on energy consumption.

claim: The excitation wave is able to travel through the whole nerve net in cutting experiments, with von Mises or uniform neurite orientation.
source: In both cases, we find that the excitation wave is able to travel through the whole nerve net, with von Mises or uniform neurite orientation (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figures 7, 8, and 9.

claim: The through-conducting property is preserved and every neuron in the network fires once, no matter how the neurons are connected.
source: This again confirms our analytical result: the through-conducting property is preserved and every neuron in the network fires once, no matter how the neurons are connected.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data in cutting experiments.

claim: Two vortex pairs are shed off near the bell margin during a swimming stroke.
source: We find indeed that two such vortex pairs are shed off near the bell margin (see Figure 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The first vortex pair is shed off during the contraction and the second one during the relaxation.
source: The first pair is shed off during the contraction and the second one during the relaxation.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The second vortex pair slips under the jellyfish bell, which provides additional forward push.
source: The second pair slips under the jellyfish bell, which provides additional forward push (Gemmell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data and citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: In the 2D model, the vortex pairs move further into the bell and interact with it for a longer time.
source: In contrast, in our 2D model, the vortex pairs move further into the bell and interact with it for a longer time.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The discrepancy between 2D model and real jellyfish vortex behavior has been observed in previous 2D models of oblate jellyfish and is likely due to the different behavior of 2D and 3D vortices.
source: This has been observed in previous 2D models of oblate jellyfish, even with prescribed bell deformation and is likely due to the different behavior of 2D and 3D vortices (Herschlag and Miller, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to peer-reviewed literature and inference.

claim: The sequence of changes in the bell geometry in the model agrees with that of real jellyfish.
source: When tracking the same data in our simulations for our standard parameters, we find qualitatively similar time series (see Figure 11 blue). In particular, the sequence of changes in the bell geometry agrees with that of real jellyfish (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model simulation data to experimental data shown in Figure 11.

claim: During the contraction phase, the bell diameter shrinks and the bell height increases in the model.
source: During the contraction phase, the bell diameter shrinks and the bell height increases.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 11.

claim: The bell margin begins to bend outward as the jellyfish contracts and folds inward during the relaxation of the bell in the model.
source: The bell margin begins to bend outward as the jellyfish contracts and folds inward during the relaxation of the bell.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 11.

claim: The margins of the real jellyfish bend less than those of the model jellyfish.
source: The margins of the real jellyfish bend less than those of our model jellyfish (Figure 11C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model simulation data to experimental data shown in Figure 11C.

claim: The higher stiffness of real jellyfish margins may originate from passive resistance of the probably inactive radial muscles.
source: Their higher stiffness may originate from passive resistance of the probably inactive radial muscles.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the cause of the discrepancy.

claim: The speed profile in the experiments shows broader peaks and a longer continuation of forward movement after bell relaxation compared to the model.
source: The speed profile in the experiments shows broader peaks and a longer continuation of forward movement after bell relaxation compared to our (Figure 11D) and previous 2D models (Herschlag and Miller, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model simulation data to experimental data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: The models produce negligible forward momentum during the relaxation phase in oblate jellyfish.
source: In particular, the models produce negligible forward momentum during the relaxation phase in oblate jellyfish.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 11D.

claim: The discrepancy in speed profile may be due to differences in vortex dynamics in 2D and 3D.
source: This may again be due to differences in vortex dynamics in 2D and 3D, as a 3D model does not show this discrepancy (Park et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and citation to peer-reviewed literature.

claim: A 2D model of oblate jellyfish is unable to reproduce the real rowing mechanism.
source: This supports the idea that a 2D model of oblate jellyfish is unable to reproduce the real rowing mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: The typical total distance traveled by individual jellyfish increases with network size.
source: We find that the typical total distance traveled by individual jellyfish increases with network size (Figure 12A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 12.

claim: The variance in distance traveled and the typical distance traveled sideways and the typical angular movement decrease with network size.
source: while the variance and thus the typical distance traveled sideways and the typical angular movement decrease (Figure 12A,C A,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 12.

claim: The effects of network size on swimming can be explained by the higher temporal and spatial coherence in the activation waves of larger MNNs.
source: This can be explained by the higher temporal and spatial coherence in the activation waves of larger MNNs.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: A simultaneous activation of the DNN and the MNN leads to a turn.
source: We find that a simultaneous activation of the DNN and the MNN indeed leads to a turn, see Figure 13.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 13.

claim: The jellyfish turns towards the origin of the contraction wave if both MNN and DNN are stimulated at the same time.
source: The jellyfish turns towards the origin of the contraction wave if both MNN and DNN are stimulated at the same time.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 13.

claim: The radial muscles of the bell margin on the stimulated side contract simultaneously with the circular muscles such that the bell margin stiffens up and does not bend outwards during the contraction of the bell.
source: The radial muscles of the bell margin on the stimulated side contract simultaneously with the circular muscles such that the bell margin stiffens up and does not bend outwards during the contraction of the bell, cf. the left hand side margin in Figure 13.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 13.

claim: Because the water resistance is increased on the stimulated side, the contraction is slowed down.
source: Because the water resistance is increased on this side, the contraction is slowed down.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: Due to the different conduction speeds of MNN and DNN, the circular muscles on the other side contract before the radial muscles.
source: Due to the different conduction speeds of MNN and DNN, the circular muscles on the other side contract before the radial muscles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: The displayed dynamics in Figure 13 are similar to those experimentally observed in Aurelia by Gemmell et al. (2015).
source: The displayed dynamics are similar to those experimentally observed in Aurelia by Gemmell et al. (2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of model simulation data to experimental observations.

claim: The jellyfish turns toward the side of initial contraction in the model.
source: In particular, the jellyfish turns toward the side of initial contraction
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 13.

claim: The bell margin on the inside of the turn is contracted while the opposing one extends outwards in the model.
source: and the bell margin on the inside of the turn is contracted while the opposing one extends outwards.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 13.

claim: For small delays between DNN and MNN activation, the jellyfish turns toward the origin of the stimulation.
source: For small delays, the jellyfish turns toward the origin of the stimulation, like for zero delay (Figure 13) and as observed by Horridge (1956) and Gemmell et al. (2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 14 and citations.

claim: As the delay between DNN and MNN activation increases, the jellyfish turns less.
source: As the delay increases, the jellyfish turns less.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 14.

claim: At a certain delay the turning direction changes, and the jellyfish turns more and more into the opposite direction.
source: At a certain delay the turning direction changes, and the jellyfish turns more and more into the opposite direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 14.

claim: For even larger delays, the jellyfish again turns less and there is eventually another change of direction.
source: For even larger delays, the jellyfish again turns less and there is eventually another change of direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 14.

claim: The points of first direction change and maximum opposite turning depend on the speed of the DNN signal.
source: The points of first direction change and maximum opposite turning depend on the speed of the DNN signal (Figure 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 14.

claim: The first change of turning direction occurs because for sufficiently large delay between DNN and MNN the radial muscles on the side of wave initiation are already relaxing when the circular muscles contract.
source: The first change of turning direction occurs because for sufficiently large delay between DNN and MNN the radial muscles on the side of wave initiation are already relaxing when the circular muscles contract, see Figure 15.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data shown in Figure 15.

claim: On the opposing side, the activity of the radial muscles coincides with the contraction of the circular muscles for sufficiently large delay.
source: On the opposing side, the activity of the radial muscles then coincides with the contraction of the circular muscles.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data shown in Figure 15.

claim: The same mechanism that causes the turn towards the initiating rhopalium for simultaneous DNN and MNN activation lets the jellyfish turn to the other side for sufficiently large delay.
source: Therefore, the same mechanism that causes the turn towards the initiating rhopalium for simultaneous DNN and MNN activation lets the jellyfish now turn to the other side.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: The jellyfish can turn away from the initiating rhopalium although both DNN and MNN are activated by the same rhopalium.
source: This occurs although both DNN and MNN are activated by the same rhopalium.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 15.

claim: The most negative angular movement occurs at a delay that is about the conduction delay of the MNN shorter than the time it takes the DNN to conduct a signal around the bell.
source: The most negative angular movement occurs at a delay that is about the conduction delay of the MNN shorter than the time it takes the DNN to conduct a signal around the bell; compare the delays at minima in Figure 14 with the corresponding DNN conduction delays in Figure 14 minus the MNN conduction delay of 35 ms.
evidence: The claim is supported by model simulation data shown in Figure 14.

claim: With such a delay, the two signals will simultaneously reach the opposing side of the bell.
source: With such a delay, the two signals will simultaneously reach the opposing side of the bell.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from model simulation data.

claim: The mechanism of turning away from the initiating rhopalium may explain how a jellyfish is able to avoid undesired stimuli.
source: This previously undescribed mechanism may explain how a jellyfish is able to avoid undesired stimuli.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation derived from model results.

claim: The pacemaker at the rhopalia may fire after an appropriate delay generated by a yet unknown mechanism, allowing the jellyfish to flee if necessary.
source: Our simulation together with the experiments by Passano (1965) and Passano (1973) let us hypothesize that the pacemaker at the rhopalia may rather fire after an appropriate delay, generated by a yet unknown mechanism. This would allow the jellyfish to flee if necessary.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation derived from model results and citations.
